content: 1. A study conducted in rural Lesotho evaluated the feasibility of cryptococcal antigen screening by non-specialist healthcare workers using a rapid diagnostic test at the point of care. This study was published in PLOS One in 2017. 2. Antifungal drug availability and distribution maps are accessible online, providing critical information on the accessibility of antifungal medications. These resources were last accessed on March 9, 2022. 3. Loyse et al. (2013) highlighted the challenges of improving access to essential antifungal medications for the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis in resource-limited settings. This work was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 4. Smilnak et al. (2018) explored a novel therapeutic approach for cryptococcal meningitis using neurapheresis therapy. Their findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) released consolidated guidelines in 2021 on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring. These guidelines emphasize a public health approach and were last accessed on March 9, 2022. 6. The Global AIDS Monitoring website provides comprehensive data on HIV/AIDS-related metrics and was last accessed on March 9, 2022. 7. Recommendations for diagnosing and managing cryptococcal meningitis have evolved over time. Initial guidelines were introduced in 2012, updated in 2018, and further revised in 2022 to reflect new evidence and best practices. 8. Cryptococcal meningitis diagnosis involves screening for cryptococcal antigen in serum or plasma using lateral flow assays or latex agglutination assays. Positive cases are followed by preemptive antifungal therapy, particularly in individuals with low CD4 cell counts. 9. Primary antifungal prophylaxis is recommended for individuals living with HIV to prevent cryptococcal disease. Treatment regimens for cryptococcal meningitis include induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases, with specific recommendations for each phase. 10. The induction phase of antifungal treatment has been consistently recommended since 2012, with updates in 2018 and 2022. Consolidation and maintenance phases are also critical components of the treatment protocol. 11. Maintenance therapy discontinuation is advised under specific clinical conditions, and adjuvant therapy with systemic corticosteroids may be considered during the induction phase. 12. The timing of antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation in individuals with cryptococcal meningitis is a critical consideration and has been addressed in the guidelines. 13. The WHO first published rapid advice on cryptococcal disease management in 2011. Subsequent updates in 2018 and 2021 incorporated new evidence on prevention, screening, and treatment strategies. 14. In February 2022, a Guideline Development Group convened to review evidence and formulate recommendations for the preferred induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis treatment. 15. The guideline development process involved systematic evidence retrieval, synthesis, and evaluation using the GRADE methodology. This approach assessed the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations. 16. The GRADE framework evaluates the extent to which reported estimates of effect are close to the actual effects of interest. It also considers the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, including health outcomes, resource use, and cost implications. 17. Systematic reviews informing the guidelines adhered to PRISMA standards for reporting. A systematic review on cryptococcal meningitis treatment was led by Adrienne Shapiro at the University of Washington. 18. Acceptability, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of treatment options were assessed through qualitative studies and sub-studies, including data from the AMBITION Trial conducted in multiple African countries. 19. Costing information for key antifungal drugs, such as amphotericin B, liposomal amphotericin B, fluconazole, and flucytosine, was compiled from sources like the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Médecins Sans Frontières. 20. The Guideline Development Group met virtually in February 2022 to finalize recommendations through consensus. Voting was not required, but a two-thirds majority was agreed upon for decision-making. 21. Draft guidelines underwent peer review by members of the Guideline Development Group and an External Review Group. Comments were incorporated into the final document, with conflicts of interest carefully managed. 22. All contributors to the guidelines completed WHO declarations of interest forms. A web-based search was conducted to identify potential competing interests, and management plans were established for any declared conflicts. 23. The External Review Group provided additional input, and their comments were considered in the finalization of the guidelines. Conflicts of interest were addressed during the review process. 24. The guideline development process and declarations of interest are documented and maintained by the WHO Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infections Programmes for a period of 10 years. 25. The guidelines aim to improve the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV, with a focus on evidence-based and resource-sensitive approaches.
